At a glance

The funnel that puts rent on a credit report.

Problem
Rent is the largest monthly expense most people have, and for renters with thin credit files it never reaches a credit report.
My part
Design owner for the end-to-end funnel: portal selection, bureau reporting logic, opt-in and opt-out states, banners, widgets and the disclosure layer.
Result
Application conversion 30% to 50% and 15% fewer related support tickets, live since March 2026.

Context

Can paying rent build your credit score?

For millions of renters with thin credit files, the answer used to be no. Rent is the largest monthly expense most people have, but it doesn't show up on a credit report unless someone actively reports it. That gap is what this project was built to close.

Rent reporting lets users connect their rent portal and have their payment history reported to credit bureaus. For the target audience, users rebuilding or starting their credit, this is one of the fastest paths to a real score improvement.

I designed the end-to-end funnel. The goal was clear: make it easy for users to start reporting, and make the value obvious before they commit.

Approach

Three layers, and the value came before the steps.

Get users in

The pitch screen needed to communicate one thing: your rent payments can count toward your credit score. No fine print first. Value first, then the steps.

Portal selection and bureau logic

Users pick their rent portal or indicate they don't have one. Reporting goes to two credit bureaus, each with different handling. The design needed to account for both paths, the transition between them, and what users see when one bureau is active and the other isn't.

Surface it everywhere it matters

Banners on the Home Tab. Widgets in the Credit Tab. Opt-out users seeing a path back in. Each touchpoint with its own state logic based on the user's reporting status.

Outcome

Conversion went from 30% to 50%.

What shipped was the full funnel: sign-up through reporting, with all bureau paths, portal selection, edge cases for users without a portal, and the widget and banner system surfacing the feature across the app.

Later, support for the second bureau was added to the funnel. A disclosure update moved the compliance layer into the Credit Tab.

Decision

I held design sign-off by a day.

Frontend had unresolved issues. The PM was pushing to close the sprint. I flagged it to the Design Director and asked to sync with engineering the next morning before releasing.

"Well done. Push for quality always." Design Director

Sign-off is the last moment design has leverage over what ships. I'd rather delay by a day than approve something I know needs fixes.

Setback

Four to six days of work took close to three weeks.

The spec had gaps and the bureau logic changed three times Missing copy and unmapped edge cases. That is what stretched a four to six day project to close to three weeks.
I designed around the gaps · mine I should have pushed for the spec first. Starting early felt productive, and reworking the same screens three times was not.
I wrote the post-mortem at the end · mine I should have written it at week two. The problems were visible earlier than I reported them.

Takeaways

What I'd do differently.

  • When a spec has gaps, push for the answers first. Starting early feels productive. Reworking the same screens three times is not.
  • The sign-off delay was right. Design sign-off is the last checkpoint before screens are locked. Using it as a quality gate is exactly what it's for.
  • Write the post-mortem at week two, not week three. Flag problems mid-project.
